design: Both SHAP and feature ablation were applied separately to BiLSTM-Attention and BU-LSTM-Attention using the same five seeds (42, 123, 7, 2024 and 99) within each architecture. Each architecture comprised five full-model runs, 35 single-variable ablation runs (seven variables by five seeds) and ten group-ablation runs (two groups by five seeds), giving 100 training runs across the two architectures. Each reduced model was paired with its full model trained with the same seed, with data partitions, preprocessing and training settings otherwise fixed within the architecture. SHAP was recomputed on those same five full models.
uncertainty: Training variability was summarized by five-seed standard deviations, pointwise 95\% Student-$t$ intervals with four degrees of freedom and counts of seeds with a positive removal effect. These seed-based summaries describe variability across five fitted models, whereas the bootstrap intervals describe test-sample uncertainty conditional on those models; neither combines all sources of uncertainty. All reported confidence intervals are pointwise 95\%, without family-wise or false-discovery-rate adjustment. For ablation, test-sample uncertainty was estimated using paired moving blocks of 28 consecutive six-hourly samples (seven days), with 10,000 replicates and resampling seed 42 specified in the archived analysis code. The same sampled blocks were used for the full and reduced configurations and across seeds; RMSE differences were calculated within each seed and then averaged, rather than first averaging predictions across seeds. For SHAP, sampling intervals used 2,000 bootstrap replicates resampling explained cases by calendar day, with resampling seed 42 specified in the code; the fixed background was not resampled. These intervals address test-case sampling uncertainty and do not evaluate sensitivity to alternative backgrounds.
shap_stability: SHAP and ablation rankings had weak agreement in the upper tail, with Kendall's $\tau=0.048$ for both architectures. For BiLSTM-Attention, the comparison between random-sample SHAP and full-test ablation rankings gave $\tau=0.524$; because those rankings use different evaluation subsets, this value is interpreted descriptively. SHAP rankings were relatively stable across seeds: for BiLSTM-Attention, mean pairwise $\tau$ was 0.733 in the random sample and 0.924 in the upper tail. Across architectures, SHAP rank agreement was 0.810 in both subsets. The separately approximated temporal attributions were concentrated toward the most recent input time, but are not substituted for the grouped exact importance values.
bi_removal: In BiLSTM-Attention, removing surface pressure (sp), total cloud cover (tcc) and 10-metre v-component of wind (v10) increased overall RMSE by 0.004022, 0.002664 and 0.002481~mm\,h$^{-1}$, respectively. Each effect was positive in all five seeds, and both its pointwise 95\% seed-$t$ and moving-block bootstrap intervals excluded zero. By contrast, removing any individual precipitation-related predictor (mxtpr, mntpr or lsp) produced only small changes, with both pointwise intervals including zero in this architecture.
bu_removal: The BU-LSTM-Attention results were less stable across training seeds. Removing tcc or sp increased RMSE in four of five seeds; their pointwise 95\% moving-block bootstrap intervals excluded zero, but their seed-$t$ intervals included zero. They are therefore not described as equally robust to the BiLSTM-Attention effects. Removing individual precipitation-related predictors sometimes improved performance; for mntpr, the overall mean difference was negative and both pointwise intervals excluded zero. Overall ablation-rank agreement across seeds was 0.867 for BiLSTM-Attention and 0.543 for BU-LSTM-Attention, further indicating architecture-dependent training variability.
group: Removing mxtpr, mntpr and lsp together from BiLSTM-Attention increased overall RMSE by 0.004805~mm\,h$^{-1}$ (pointwise 95\% moving-block bootstrap interval: 0.001980 to 0.008062) and upper-tail RMSE by 0.019359~mm\,h$^{-1}$ (pointwise 95\% moving-block bootstrap interval: 0.005695 to 0.034165). Both effects were positive in all five seeds. Removing mxtpr and mntpr while retaining lsp changed performance little in this architecture. These findings support overlapping predictive information among the precipitation-related variables: removing one can leave useful information in the remaining inputs, whereas removing the group reduces predictive utility. They do not establish meteorological causality or universal necessity.
